item.title: Energy-Aware Performance Characterization of Kokkos Kernels Across Precision Levels
item.description: arXiv:2610.31917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kokkos is a performance-portable programming model used in GPU-accelerated HPC applications comprising kernels with diverse computational and memory behaviors. We characterize kernels from two applications to evaluate how FP32, FP64, and mixed FP32/FP64 affect arithmetic intensity, performance throughput, and GPU energy consumption. We introduce an Energy-Aware Roofline Model that incorporates energy into performance analysis and a Thermal-Aware Inter-Kernel Energy Model that visualizes energy consumption alongside duration, GPU temperature, and execution order. We study both applications with: (1) fine-grained, application-level instrumentation through the Kokkos Performance Tools PAPI Connector and (2) coarse-grained PAPI instrumentation applied to a dedicated-kernel benchmark using vendor-specific power management components. Our analysis shows that precision effects vary by application, kernel, and workload. Mixed FP32/FP64 kernels generally achieve arithmetic intensity comparable to FP32, with modestly lower throughput and, in most cases, a modest increase in energy consumption. FP64 kernels generally exhibit the highest energy consumption among the evaluated precision configurations.
item.dc:creator: Maria Patrou, Andrey Prokopenko, Aditya Kashi, Oscar Hernandez, Jean-Luc Fattebert

item.title: Measuring the Energy Cost of Completing Tasks with Quantized Language-Model Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.32417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and energy needed to serve large language models (LLMs) and AI agents for coding and data analysis can now run on locally hosted LLMs. In practice, this benefit is commonly benchmarked per output token. Yet an agent calls its model repeatedly, runs tools, and revises its work, and quantization can change both how much the agent generates and whether it succeeds. Existing energy studies either compare quantized models on single requests or measure agents at one fixed precision, overlooking how a change in precision plays out across a complete agent task. To address this gap, this paper presents the first characterization of the task-level energy trade-offs of model quantization in locally hosted agents. We develop 29 agent tasks with automatic pass/fail checks in six families, ranging from single-answer SQL analytics to multi-step repository bug fixing, and measure CPU and GPU energy per output token and per completed task for 4-bit and 8-bit versions of two open-weight models on bare-metal NVIDIA A100 nodes with llama.cpp. Our findings reveal that 4-bit precision generally saves energy per token, though whether it saves energy per completed task is task dependent and changes with the model and the execution budget (i.e., limits on turns, tokens, and time). We trace this discrepancy to the extra tokens needed to complete a task in full, which translates into using up to 3.5 times as much energy per completed task. These findings offer actionable guidance for developers and operators choosing model precision for agents, showing how tokens per completed task, set against the per-token saving, reveal whether lower precision completes the work with less energy.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Abkin, Aldric Yang, Alex Flesher, Nitheesh Kodarapu, Deepak Panigrahy, Aakash Tyagi, David Kebo Houngninou

item.title: Toward Open ISA Supercomputing: A Comparative Study of RISC-V, Arm, and x86 Architectures on HPC Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2610.32632v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: RISC-V is emerging as a candidate architecture for high-performance computing (HPC), but its competitiveness against established x86 and Arm processors remains difficult to assess because existing studies use different platforms, workloads, and methodologies, and rarely consider energy efficiency. Our work provides an evaluation of contemporary HPC RISC-V, Arm, and x86 processors using a common software stack and methodology. We characterize the Sophgo SG2044 and compare it with the NVIDIA Grace CPU Superchip and Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ across four HPC benchmarks (STREAM, HPL, HPL-MxP, and HPCG) and four representative applications (iPIC3D, PLUTO, OpenFOAM, and llama.cpp). The version of HPL-MxP linked to OpenBLAS built and used for this work is made available as open-source software. The SG2044 reaches 8.02 GFLOP/s of FP64 performance and 7.8 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core, increasing to 294 GFLOP/s and 107 GB/s at 64 cores. L2-cache-aware process placement enables near-linear scaling up to 16 cores, beyond which memory-bandwidth saturation limits further gains. Across generations of RISC-V hardware, in the context of the Monte Cimone (MC) project, the SG2044-based MCv3 doubles both single-core performance and peak memory bandwidth relative to MCv2, while improving memory bandwidth, node-level FP64 performance, and energy efficiency by approximately 100x, 158x, and 10x, over MCv1. Against the Arm and x86 systems, the SG2044 shows 8-15x less absolute performance, reflecting its narrower vector resources and less advanced technology node, but delivers competitive scaling and energy efficiency on several workloads. Its most notable result is LLM decode, where 64-core execution provides the highest relative scaling and energy efficiency among the evaluated platforms while exceeding Intel in throughput. Our results show that RISC-V processors are closing the gap with the competition.
item.dc:creator: Emanuele Venieri, Giacomo Madella, Gabriele Ceccolini, Simone Manoni, Federico Ficarelli, Filippo Barbari, Jenny Lynn Almerol, Elisabetta Boella, Nitin Shukla, Simone Bn\`a, Luca Benini, Andrea bartolini

item.title: Cluster, Route, Escalate: Cascaded Framework for Cost-Aware LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2606.27457v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Serving open-weight language models on premises forces a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. Hosting models of different sizes lets easy queries go to a small, efficient model and hard ones to a large model. We present CRE-Router (Cluster, Route, Escalate), a two-stage method that decides which of these models answers each query. It clusters queries and routes each cluster to the model that best trades error against cost, under a budget on the time per output token (TPOT) or the end-to-end latency per request (E2EL). It then either accepts the answer or, when a quality estimator rejects it, escalates the query to the strong model. Routing decides before generation, so a hard query goes straight to the strong model; escalation decides after, so it can catch the errors routing cannot predict. It needs no annotation beyond task-correctness labels. We evaluate CRE-Router on TeleMath, TeleQnA and AIME, with pools of two to nine models served on A100 GPUs. CRE-Router is more accurate than the efficient models in its pool and comparable to the strong model it escalates to, at a lower cost per token. We also find that the choice of cost term decides which models serve the workload, that pricing each model per cluster shortens the wait per request, and that a change of hardware changes the best routing.
item.dc:creator: Yasmin Moslem, Magdalena Kacmajor, Vasudevan Nedumpozhimana, Ammar Abbas, Solmaz Panahi, David Lynch, Zhuangzhuang Nie, Alexandros Agapitos, Aleksandar Milenovic, Hongmeng Song, Yucheng Shi, Yue Pan, Patricia Buffini, John D. Kelleher

item.title: A Reduced Stochastic Model of Microservice Availability: Algorithms for Identification and Formal Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2607.00740v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Estimating microservice operation availability requires connecting runtime observations to completion of the required work within a deadline. Detailed architectural models provide one route, but their reconstruction and analysis can be costly. We present algorithms for identifying and analysing a reduced stochastic availability model from telemetry and declared operation requirements. The identification procedure constructs a joint law of execution states and retains compatible laws when observations are incomplete. Formal results establish attainable probability bounds and conditions for identifying a completion-and-deadline representation directly. This construction preserves the range obtained by evaluating the same completion-and-deadline event in the full model; a separate joint comparison describes the structural information discarded. An independent study covered three microservice applications and 18 campaigns. On complete common campaigns with point forecasts from both methods, observed mean absolute errors differed from those of independently extracted PMX/Palladio architectural models by at most 0.082 percentage points. The full graph-based workflow from telemetry to first forecast was 31.73-100.24 times faster than the studied PMX/Palladio workflow, including startup and launcher waits. Direct identification preserved the retained forecasts and intervals, with median paired first-answer savings of 5.1-11.2% relative to full execution-model analysis. The results connect required model detail to measured identification and analysis costs.
item.dc:creator: Anatoly A. Krasnovsky, Anna Maslovskaya

item.title: TreeWY: Speculative Verification for Gated DeltaNet Hybrids
item.description: arXiv:2608.20961v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern open models are hybrids: most layers are linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet, GDN) layers carrying a small fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value (KV) cache. This makes ordinary decoding memory-efficient, but hurts speculative decoding. To verify a batch of draft tokens and then roll back the rejected ones, today's systems snapshot the full recurrent state at every draft position for GDN layers, and those snapshots cannot be shared across branches of a draft tree, so a wide, high-acceptance tree becomes memory-infeasible. We remove the snapshots. Using a tree-structured WY transform of the gated delta rule, we compute every draft node's output with a single triangular solve and reconstruct only the one accepted state on commit, storing a small pseudo-value matrix instead of per-node states; the derivation depends only on the gated delta rule, not on any other architectural detail. In serving benchmarks on two scales of one hybrid model family (Qwen3.5 35B and 397B) this cuts speculative recurrent-state memory and KV-cache pressure at essentially identical acceptance length, turning the freed HBM into higher throughput and much lower time-to-first-token (TTFT) wherever memory binds, and costing a few percent where it does not. For tree width the same memory buys affordability: a wider, higher-acceptance draft becomes possible, though not yet a throughput win.
item.dc:creator: Sneha Murthy Ghantasala

item.title: MLIPS: Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing
item.description: arXiv:2610.27438v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse attention limits the keys used by each query, but finding those keys can still require a full-prefix scan at every layer. We introduce $MLIPS:$ $Multi$-$Layer$ $Indexer$ $Pool$ $Sharing$, a training-free method that shares candidate search while retaining each consumer's own scoring and selection. A producer publishes a top-$M$ pool larger than the attention budget $K$; subsequent layers select their own top-$K$ from that pool. Measurements across three sparse-attention model families show substantially higher coverage from broad pools than overlap between final selections. We implement layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Across four long-context suites, three consumer layers per producer give $1.14$-$1.40\times$ speedups and $14.8$-$27.4\%$ lower GPU energy, with observed accuracy changes of $-1.49$ to $+0.29$ percentage points in single runs. More extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. Sampled prefill traces also reveal recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers. We characterize this shared working-set structure and use it to motivate Top-$G$, an exploratory bounded pool construction for prefill. Its deployment, task accuracy, and serving benefits remain open.
item.dc:creator: Samkit Jain, Sai Kishan Pampana, Shlok Agarwal, Yashwant Marathe, Bhargava Gopireddy, Aradhana Mohan Parvathy, Sachin Idgunji
